# Heedfulness Is the Path to the Deathless

*Dhp 21-32, the Appamādavagga — set 2, The Basic Diagnosis and the Path*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 2 min · 303 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

This page is a short chapter of verses from the Dhammapada, the best-known
collection of the Buddha's sayings. All twelve verses are about one quality:
*heedfulness*.

Heedfulness means not drifting. It is the quality of someone who stays
awake to what they are doing, keeps making the effort, and comes back
when attention slips. Its opposite, heedlessness, is simply letting
things slide.

The first verse makes the whole claim at once: heedfulness is the path to
the deathless, and heedlessness is the path to death. The rest show what
that looks like: a person building an island no flood can reach, a fire
burning up its fetters, someone on a mountain looking out over the plain.

The numbers beside the verses are the Dhammapada's own verse numbers, so
you can find any verse in other translations. *Maghavā*, in verse 30, is a
name of Sakka, the chief of the devas.

## Translation

### Verses

<span class="verse-number">21</span><span class="verse-line">Heedfulness is the path to the deathless;</span>
<span class="verse-line">heedlessness is the path to death.</span>
<span class="verse-line">The heedful do not die;</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">the heedless are as if already dead.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">22</span><span class="verse-line">Knowing this difference clearly,</span>
<span class="verse-line">the wise, established in heedfulness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">rejoice in heedfulness,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">delighting in the range of the noble ones.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">23</span><span class="verse-line">Those who practice the mental themes, persevering,</span>
<span class="verse-line">always firm in their effort,</span>
<span class="verse-line">the steadfast touch nibbāna,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">the unsurpassed security from the yoke.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">24</span><span class="verse-line">For someone who is energetic and remembers,</span>
<span class="verse-line">whose actions are clean, who acts with care,</span>
<span class="verse-line">who is restrained, living by the Dhamma,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">and heedful, fame grows.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">25</span><span class="verse-line">By effort and heedfulness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">by restraint and self-control,</span>
<span class="verse-line">the intelligent should make an island</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">that no flood can overwhelm.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">26</span><span class="verse-line">Fools, people of poor understanding,</span>
<span class="verse-line">give themselves to heedlessness;</span>
<span class="verse-line">the intelligent guard heedfulness</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">as their greatest treasure.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">27</span><span class="verse-line">Do not give yourselves to heedlessness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">nor to intimacy with sensual delight.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Whoever is heedful and practices the mental themes</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">reaches abundant satisfaction.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">28</span><span class="verse-line">When the wise drive out heedlessness</span>
<span class="verse-line">by heedfulness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">they climb the tower of discernment,</span>
<span class="verse-line">and free of sorrow, they look out over a sorrowing people,</span>
<span class="verse-line">as one standing on a mountain looks out over those on the plain:</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">the steadfast look out over fools.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">29</span><span class="verse-line">Heedful among the heedless,</span>
<span class="verse-line">wide awake among those asleep,</span>
<span class="verse-line">the person of good understanding goes on ahead,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">as a swift horse leaves a weak one behind.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">30</span><span class="verse-line">By heedfulness Maghavā</span>
<span class="verse-line">rose to be chief of the devas.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Heedfulness is praised;</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">heedlessness is always blamed.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">31</span><span class="verse-line">A bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">or who sees fear in heedlessness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">goes on like a fire,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">burning up every fetter, fine or coarse.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">32</span><span class="verse-line">A bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">or who sees fear in heedlessness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">cannot fall away:</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">they are close to nibbāna.</span>
{: .verse }

The second chapter, on heedfulness, is finished.

*[bhikkhu]: A Buddhist monk -- someone who has left household life to practise full time. Left untranslated because "monk" carries centuries of unrelated European associations.
*[deathless]: A name for nibbāna: what does not die, because it was never born.
*[Dhamma]: The Buddha's teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.
*[flood]: A force that overwhelms and carries a person along unless it is crossed. SN 1.1 leaves the image open rather than defining it as one specific mental state.
*[heedful]: Living with heedfulness: awake to what you are doing and keeping up the effort.
*[heedfulness]: This project's rendering of "appamāda" -- staying awake to what you are doing, keeping up the effort, and coming back when attention slips. Often translated "diligence" or "vigilance."
*[heedlessness]: The opposite of heedfulness: drifting, letting things slide, not noticing what the mind is doing.
*[nibbāna]: The end of greed, hatred, and confusion -- the traditional goal of Buddhist practice. Left untranslated because no single English word covers it; "quenching" is the closest one-word gloss.
*[security from the yoke]: A name for nibbāna: safety from the yokes of sensuality, becoming, views, and ignorance that bind a person to further becoming.
